name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Implement a shared "Decision Log" artifact where every department records their key choices and the reasons behind them. This single artifact will cut cross-team confusion by making trade-offs visible to everyone at a glance. Product and Engineering will own it—Product sets the format for clarity, Engineering enforces the discipline of logging every non-trivial decision. The trade-off is slower initial documentation for faster alignment later.

name: Scriv
text: The shared "Decision Log" risks becoming a graveyard of stale entries no one reads—unless we enforce a strict sunset rule: every log entry expires in 90 days unless renewed by the owner. Engineering should own the artifact itself; Product should only define the *fields* required for clarity, not the format. A 48-hour review cycle where a rotating cross-team pair verifies entries are still actionable would settle it.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt the shared "Decision Log" with a 90-day sunset rule enforced by Engineering. This forces every team to revisit their entries, keeping the log alive and useful instead of a dusty archive. The trade-off is that teams must spend a few minutes every quarter to renew or retire entries, but that small cost prevents the bigger waste of ignored or outdated decisions.

name: Sift
text: The 90-day sunset rule turns the Decision Log into a chore—teams will dump half-baked entries just to clear the deadline, not to inform others. Instead, make renewal opt-in: Engineering builds a lightweight "active log" view that only surfaces decisions still in play, letting stale entries fade into the background. Settle it by running a two-week pilot with one team; if renewal rates drop below 30%, we’ll know the opt-in model works better.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the shared "Decision Log" with a 90-day sunset rule enforced by Engineering. This forces teams to actively curate entries, ensuring the log stays relevant and not a static archive. The trade-off is the quarterly renewal effort, but it prevents the log from becoming noise. Engineering owns the enforcement; Product defines the clarity fields.

name: Scriv
text: The 90-day sunset rule still risks teams gaming the system—dumping entries just to clear the deadline—while the opt-in "active log" view lets stale decisions linger unchecked. Instead, enforce renewal only for decisions that *directly impact* other teams, with Engineering flagging these for review. That keeps the log alive without turning it into a quarterly scramble.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the shared "Decision Log" with a 90-day sunset rule enforced by Engineering, but limit renewal to decisions that *directly impact other teams*. Engineering builds a lightweight flagging system to identify cross-team impact, so only those entries require renewal—everyone else can let theirs fade. The trade-off is that teams must spend time flagging decisions correctly upfront, but this keeps the log focused on what actually matters to others.

name: Scriv
text: The flagging system adds hidden complexity—Engineering now owns a second rule to enforce, and teams will still game it by mislabeling impact. Instead, enforce a simpler rule: every log entry must cite a *specific* future decision it constrains, or it auto-expires. This shifts the burden from renewal to clarity, and the artifact itself becomes the enforcement mechanism. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with one cross-team decision—if the cited constraint is missing, the entry dies.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the "specific future decision" rule: every Decision Log entry must cite a concrete future decision it constrains, or it auto-expires. This forces teams to think critically about why an entry matters, cutting noise without adding renewal chores. The trade-off is that teams must frame entries in terms of future impact, which may slow down initial logging—but it guarantees the log stays useful, not just busywork.

name: Sift
text: The "specific future decision" rule assumes teams can predict their own constraints—what if a decision’s value isn’t obvious until months later, like a security patch or compliance change? Instead, enforce a rolling *impact review*: every entry auto-expires unless a reviewer from another team explicitly vouches for its ongoing relevance. Engineering builds a one-click "still matters" button; if no one clicks, it dies. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with two teams—if the log shrinks without real losses, adopt it.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the "specific future decision" rule for the Decision Log: every entry must cite a concrete future decision it constrains, or it auto-expires after 90 days. This forces teams to justify why a decision matters *now*, cutting noise without adding renewal chores or hidden complexity. The trade-off is that teams must frame entries in terms of actionable constraints—some contextual decisions (like security patches) may expire prematurely, but the log stays lean and relevant. Engineering implements the auto-expiry logic; no manual flagging or reviewer gatekeeping needed.

name: Scriv
text: The "specific future decision" rule assumes teams can predict their own constraints—what if a decision’s value isn’t obvious until months later, like a security patch or compliance change? Instead, enforce a rolling *impact review*: every entry auto-expires unless a reviewer from another team explicitly confirms its ongoing relevance. The lead for this is Engineering, and the artifact is a lightweight review calendar with clear escalation paths.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the "specific future decision" rule for the Decision Log: every entry must cite a concrete future decision it constrains, or it auto-expires after 90 days. This forces teams to justify why a decision matters *now*, cutting noise without adding renewal chores or hidden complexity. The trade-off is that teams must frame entries in terms of *known* constraints, accepting that some long-term or emergent impacts (like security patches) may get pruned—but the clarity gained outweighs the risk. Engineering owns the enforcement via a simple script that flags entries without citations.

name: Scriv
text: The "specific future decision" rule still assumes teams can predict *which* future decisions will matter—security patches and compliance changes often emerge from unplanned crises, not roadmaps. Instead, enforce a *time-boxed exception review*: entries auto-expire after 90 days unless a cross-team reviewer explicitly extends them, proving the entry’s ongoing relevance. The lead for this is the Compliance team—they already track regulatory changes and can validate whether an entry’s impact is latent or expired.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the "specific future decision" rule for the Decision Log: every entry must cite a concrete future decision it constrains, or it auto-expires after 90 days. This forces teams to justify why a decision matters now, cutting noise without adding renewal chores. The trade-off is that teams must frame entries in terms of *known* future decisions, accepting that some long-term constraints (like security patches) may expire before they’re needed.

name: Sift
text: The "time-boxed exception review" still outsources judgment to reviewers who may lack context—what if a compliance change’s urgency isn’t visible until a crisis hits? Instead, enforce a *triggered impact audit*: every Decision Log entry auto-expires unless the team that owns the future decision explicitly reaffirms its value within 90 days. That shifts accountability to the decision-maker, not a reviewer. The argument settles when the team owning the future decision states whether the entry is still relevant or should be retired.

name: Scope
text: Run Arcads AI Video’s "AI Marketing" skill pack on the target video. This will generate a 15-second teaser optimized for social platforms, cutting manual editing time by 70%. The trade-off is we lose creative control over pacing and tone—accept it because speed to market beats perfection for short-form content.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "AI Marketing" skill pack outsources brand voice to an algorithm—what if the teaser’s tone clashes with a campaign we’re already running? Instead, run a *controlled A/B test*: generate two teasers, one with the skill pack and one manual, and measure click-through rates. The artifact is the test results; the decision is which version ships.

name: Reel
text: Run Arcads AI Video’s "AI Marketing" skill pack on the target video. It cuts teaser production from hours to minutes, which matters more than brand voice for short-form content where speed beats perfection. The trade-off is we lose control over pacing and tone—accept it because social platforms reward immediacy over polish. The artifact is the 15-second teaser delivered within one day.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk isn’t brand voice—it’s that the skill pack’s "optimized for social" output will lock us into a single platform’s algorithmic bias. Instead, run a *platform-agnostic teaser*: generate three 15-second cuts (one manual, two skill pack variants) and test them on TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube Shorts. The artifact is the A/B test results; the decision is which cut to push.

name: Chisel
text: Run a *controlled A/B test* on the teaser variants: one manual, one skill-pack default, and one platform-agnostic variant. This forces data over assumptions and reveals which approach actually drives engagement across channels. The trade-off is a 24-hour delay for the test, but it beats guessing or locking into a single algorithm’s bias.
